prerequisite_refresher.title: Refresher: first variation and integration by parts
prerequisite_refresher.content:
## Functionals from the preceding page

The page before this one defines the numerator functional

$$
F[y]=\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\left(\rho(x)\,y'(x)^2+\sigma(x)\,y(x)^2\right)\,dx
$$

and the normalization functional

$$
G[y]=\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}w(x)\,y(x)^2\,dx.
$$

The Sturm–Liouville variational problem minimizes $F[y]$ subject to $G[y]=1$. The endpoint values of $y$ are fixed. Consequently an admissible variation $y_\varepsilon=y+\varepsilon\eta$ obeys $\eta(\alpha)=\eta(\beta)=0$.

## Why integration by parts gives the Euler–Lagrange equation

For a functional with density $f(x,y,y')$, its first variation is

$$
\delta F=\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\left(f_y\,\eta+f_{y'}\,\eta'\right)\,dx.
$$

Integrating the $\eta'$ term by parts gives

$$
\delta F=\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\left(f_y-\frac{d}{dx}f_{y'}\right)\eta\,dx+\left[f_{y'}\eta\right]_{\alpha}^{\beta}.
$$

The endpoint contribution vanishes here because the endpoint values are fixed, so $\eta(\alpha)=\eta(\beta)=0$. If the endpoints were free, that boundary term could not be discarded without an additional boundary condition. Since $\eta$ is otherwise arbitrary, stationarity requires

$$
f_y-\frac{d}{dx}f_{y'}=0.
$$

For the quadratic derivative term, the specific integration-by-parts step is

$$
\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\rho(x)y'(x)\eta'(x)\,dx=-\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\bigl(\rho(x)y'(x)\bigr)'\eta(x)\,dx,
$$

where the omitted endpoint term is $[\rho y'\eta]_{\alpha}^{\beta}=0$ under the same fixed-endpoint condition.

units.title: 1. Vary the constrained quadratic functionals

metadata.source_locator: printed p. 29, from ‘Let’s consider separately…’ through equation (7.3)

units.content:
### Source text (faithful transcription)

Let’s consider separately the variations of $F$ and $G$ with respect to a variation of $y(x)$:

$$
\delta F = 2\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\delta y\{-(\rho y')' + \sigma y\}\,dx - 2[\delta y\,\rho y']_{\alpha}^{\beta},
$$

$$
\delta G = 2\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\delta y\,w y\,dx.
$$

The boundary term in $\delta F$ is zero because of the fixed-end boundary conditions, so

$$
\frac{\delta F}{\delta y}=2\mathcal{L}y,\qquad \frac{\delta G}{\delta y}=2wy,
$$

where $\mathcal{L}$ is the differential operator

$$
\mathcal{L}=-\frac{d}{dx}\left(\rho(x)\frac{d}{dx}\right)+\sigma(x).
$$

In other words, $\mathcal{L}y=-(\rho y')'+\sigma y$ for any (twice-differentiable) function $y$. The EL equation (7.2) is therefore

$$
(7.3)\qquad \mathcal{L}y=\lambda w y.
$$

This is an eigenvalue problem, with eigenvalue $\lambda$. The function $w(x)$ is called a “weight function”. Many important ODEs are of Sturm-Liouville form, and one can find tables of the equations and their weight functions in texts on mathematical methods.

### Why these variations give an eigenvalue equation

The derivative term is where the operator comes from. Varying $\int\rho(y')^2 dx$ produces $2\int\rho y'\delta y' dx$; integration by parts moves the derivative off the variation and gives $-2\int(\rho y')'\delta y dx$, plus endpoint contribution (sign correction below). The fixed endpoint values make $\delta y=0$ there, so that term disappears. The non-derivative terms contribute $2\sigma y$ and $2wy$. Substituting these functional derivatives into the constrained stationarity condition $\delta F/\delta y-\lambda\delta G/\delta y=0$ yields $\mathcal{L}y=\lambda wy$.

### Interpretation and assumptions

This is a weighted eigenproblem: $\lambda$ is the eigenvalue, $y$ its eigenfunction, and multiplication by $w(x)$ weights the right side. The page assumes real coefficients, $\rho,w>0$ in the open interval, and fixed endpoint values for $y$. The integration-by-parts expression is valid for sufficiently smooth $y$ (the page states twice differentiable).

### Source-page markup and a sign check (yellow explanation)

The source page has handwritten derivation notes and colored marks. These are imported as historical source markup, not current learner checks; their dates are unknown. In the printed first-variation line above, the endpoint term is written with a minus sign: $-2[\delta y\,\rho y']_{\alpha}^{\beta}$. Direct integration by parts gives a plus sign, $+2[\delta y\,\rho y']_{\alpha}^{\beta}$, because $\int 2\rho y'\delta y' dx=2[\rho y'\delta y]_{\alpha}^{\beta}-2\int(\rho y')'\delta y dx$. The discrepancy does not change the functional derivative or equation (7.3), since $\delta y=0$ at both fixed endpoints and the boundary term vanishes either way.

units.title: 2. The lowest eigenvalue as a minimum quotient

metadata.source_locator: printed p. 29, from ‘If the function σ(x)…’ through ‘lowest SL eigenvalue’

units.content:
### Source text (faithful transcription)

If the function $\sigma(x)$ is positive then $F\geq 0$, so its minimum is positive. Its minimum value is the lowest eigenvalue of the associated Sturm-Liouville eigenvalue problem. This can be seen as follows. Multiply both sides of (7.3) by $y$ and integrate to get

$$
\lambda G=\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}y\mathcal{L}y\,dx=F-[\rho y y']_{\alpha}^{\beta},
$$

where the second equality comes from an integration by parts. The boundary term is zero, so $\lambda=F/G\geq 0$. The original problem is equivalent to the problem of minimising $F/G$ because the scale fixed by the normalization constraint drops out of this ratio, so the lowest eigenvalue will be the minimum of $F/G$.

### Derivation, one step at a time

Start with $\mathcal{L}y=\lambda wy$, multiply pointwise by $y$, and integrate: $\int y\mathcal{L}y\,dx=\lambda\int wy^2 dx=\lambda G$. For the left side,

$$
\int y[-(\rho y')'+\sigma y]dx = -[\rho yy']_{\alpha}^{\beta}+\int\rho(y')^2dx+\int\sigma y^2dx = F-[\rho yy']_{\alpha}^{\beta}.
$$

Fixed endpoint values do not, by themselves, imply $y(\alpha)=y(\beta)=0$. The boundary term vanishes here because the admissible eigenfunctions satisfy homogeneous endpoint conditions (as the source page’s handwritten note also points out). Under those boundary conditions, $\lambda=F/G$. Since $G=1$ is a normalization, rescaling a nonzero trial function changes $F$ and $G$ by the same factor $c^2$; it does not change $F/G$. Thus minimizing the constrained $F$ is equivalent to minimizing this quotient.

### Intuition and assumptions

The quotient is a weighted energy per weighted squared amplitude. Its stationary values are eigenvalues, and its minimum over admissible functions is the lowest eigenvalue. For nonzero $y$ with $w>0$, $G>0$. The claim of strict positivity requires the positivity assumptions stated on the page: in particular $\sigma>0$ together with $\rho>0$, and admissible nonzero functions. Boundary conditions must remove the boundary contribution; arbitrary fixed nonzero endpoint values would not generally make $[\rho yy']$ vanish.

units.title: 3. Vary the quotient directly

metadata.source_locator: printed p. 29, from ‘Notice that F/G…’ to end of printed page

units.content:
### Source text (faithful transcription)

Notice that $F/G$ is not a functional of the type considered so far because it is a ratio of definite integrals. Nevertheless, it is still a functional. We can solve the problem directly by minimising $\Lambda=F/G$ without constraint. The functional $\Lambda[y]$ is stationary when

$$
0=\frac{\delta\Lambda}{\delta y}=\frac{1}{G}\left[\frac{\delta F[y]}{\delta y(x)}-\frac{F}{G}\frac{\delta G[y]}{\delta y(x)}\right]=\frac{2}{G}[\mathcal{L}y-\Lambda wy],
$$

so the values of $\Lambda$ at its stationary points are the Sturm-Liouville eigenvalues, and the minimum value of $\Lambda$ is the lowest SL eigenvalue, in agreement with the conclusion above deduced using the Lagrange multiplier method.

### Quotient-rule derivation

Vary $\Lambda=F/G$ as an ordinary ratio, remembering that both numerator and denominator depend on the function: $\delta(F/G)=(G\,\delta F-F\,\delta G)/G^2$. Divide by $\delta y(x)$ and use $\delta F/\delta y=2\mathcal{L}y$ and $\delta G/\delta y=2wy$. Since $F/G=\Lambda$, this becomes $\delta\Lambda/\delta y=(2/G)(\mathcal{L}y-\Lambda wy)$. A stationary function therefore solves the same eigenvalue equation with eigenvalue $\Lambda$.

### What the two arguments each establish

The multiplier method starts from the normalization constraint and identifies stationary constrained functions. The quotient method removes the irrelevant overall scale and reaches the same equation directly. Together they show that the quotient’s stationary values are eigenvalues; the variational minimum selects the lowest one, subject to the stated admissibility and boundary conditions. This is a variational characterization, not a claim that every eigenfunction minimizes the quotient.
